name: Trofinetide
lead: Trofinetide (brand names Daybue, Daybue Stix; Daybu in the EU) is an oral prescription medicine for Rett syndrome, a rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorder, in patients aged two years and older. The US FDA approved it in March 2023, the first drug approved for the condition.[7][11][12]

It is a synthetic analogue of glycine-proline-glutamate (GPE), the N-terminal tripeptide of IGF-1, and was developed by Neuren Pharmaceuticals and then commercialised by Acadia Pharmaceuticals.[1][11] It was first explored for neuroprotection, for example in stroke.[11] Its approval rests on a 12-week placebo-controlled phase 3 trial.[1] It is a treatment for a specific disease; no source reviewed documents an appearance-related use.

paras: Trofinetide is indicated for Rett syndrome, caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene and characterised by regression after early development, loss of hand skills, seizures, breathing abnormalities and intellectual disability.[6][12] It has orphan drug, fast track and priority review designations in the US and is described as a first-in-class medication.[11]

In the phase 3 LAVENDER study, 187 females with Rett syndrome received trofinetide (93) or placebo (94) for 12 weeks. The trial reported improvement over placebo on its coprimary measures, the caregiver-rated Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire and the clinician-rated Clinical Global Impression-Improvement scale.[1][5][12] Earlier phase 2 studies in adolescent and adult and in pediatric patients established tolerability and signals of clinical benefit.[3][4]

The most common adverse effects are diarrhea and vomiting; Grokipedia reports diarrhea in 82% and vomiting in 29% of trial participants, and decreased appetite is also noted.[11][12] Product information is reported not to recommend use in moderate to severe renal impairment because of limited data.[12]

Trofinetide is a modified form of GPE with a longer half-life. In preclinical models it is reported to engage IGF-1 receptor-associated signalling pathways and to reduce neuroinflammation; it does not correct the underlying MECP2 mutation.[12][9]

The compound derives from IGF-1 neuroprotection research, was first studied for stroke, and then moved to Rett syndrome under Neuren, with Acadia running the pivotal trial.[11][12] The FDA approved it in March 2023, Health Canada followed in 2024 per Grokipedia, and a powder formulation was approved in late 2025 per Wikipedia.[11][12][7]

Randomized trials include the 2023 phase 3 study in Rett syndrome, phase 2 studies in pediatric and in adolescent/adult Rett syndrome, and a phase 2 placebo-controlled study in Fragile X syndrome.[1][3][4][8] Open-label extension and younger-age studies were registered, some terminated.[13][14] Reviews place it among emerging targeted treatments for neurodevelopmental conditions.[2]

timeline.event: Phase 2 study in adolescent and adult Rett syndrome published.[4]
Phase 2 pediatric Rett syndrome study published.[3]
Phase 3 results published; FDA approval in March.[1][11]

card.summary: The first approved Rett syndrome drug, a GPE analogue; a disease treatment with no appearance use documented.
card.note: Approved only for Rett syndrome; common GI side effects.

quick.overview:
Trofinetide is an oral prescription drug for Rett syndrome. It is a stabilised copy of a small IGF-1 fragment and was approved by the US FDA in 2023.

It entered peptide catalogues because of its relation to GPE, but its evidence concerns a rare neurological disease, not appearance.
quick.mechanism: It is thought to dampen neuroinflammation and support neuronal signalling through IGF-1-related pathways, without fixing the gene mutation behind Rett syndrome.[12]
quick.risks: Diarrhea and vomiting are the most common adverse effects in trials.[11][12] It is prescription-only, with limited data in kidney impairment.
